extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians (faculty, graduate students), and mathematicians considering using MathOverflow
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for asking and answering focused research-level mathematical questions on the MathOverflow Stack Exchange site, including what makes a good or bad question, formatting tips, and how community moderation works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimize for focused questions with clear answers
rubrics_metrics.description: MathOverflow is optimized for focused questions which (could) have clear answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site is awkward for broad or open-ended questions; use MathOverflow only when it is the right tool for the job. The software and community are tuned to make it easy to sort out the good stuff via voting; the searchable archive is valuable. If a problem is broad or open-ended, consider other venues (blogs, wikis, or other Stack Exchange sites).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best questions include motivation, background, and a clear goal
rubrics_metrics.description: The best questions for the site include motivation and background and have a clear goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context so experts can understand why the question matters and what counts as a satisfactory answer. A focused goal makes it easier for respondents to give precise answers and for the community to judge quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid discussions, homework problems, and broad requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussions, homework questions, and broad requests are not appropriate for MathOverflow and should be directed to more suitable websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MathOverflow fills a different niche than blogs (discussions) or wikis (exposition). Homework-like or overly broad questions are politely redirected elsewhere; such posts are considered a poor fit even if mathematically interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a “bad question”
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'bad question' is one which is either irrelevant to mathematicians or one where it is unclear what constitutes an answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions should be clearly relevant to mathematical research/audience and must specify what would count as an answer. If relevance or answer criteria are unclear, the community may close or downvote the question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical sophistication expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Users should expect a high level of mathematical sophistication on MathOverflow: many participants are faculty and graduate students, including leading researchers, and the mathematics can be quite advanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New visitors are often surprised by the sophistication; this affects what questions are appropriate and how answers are written. Some areas are disproportionately represented, and the site will mature over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community moderation via voting and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The community moderates itself: users vote on questions and answers, and reputation (points) measures increased privileges to make decisions about the site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upvotes increase reputation; as reputation grows users can vote, create tags, edit other people's posts, and vote to close questions. This shares moderation duties among the most active users and helps surface quality content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experienced-user privileges (editing and closing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Established members gain increased power to organize and improve the site: create tags, edit others' posts, and vote to close bad questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderation duties are efficiently shared among the most active users. Gaining these privileges is tied to reputation earned via community votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tags to navigate specialty areas
rubrics_metrics.description: If the main page is overwhelming, go to the tags page and click on a tag corresponding to your specialty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tags help focus on areas of interest; current coverage of areas is uneven, but the tag system makes it easy to jump into relevant subcommunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting mathematical notation with dollar signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical symbols, entered as between dollar signs, are automatically rendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inline LaTeX delimited by $...$ for proper mathematical typesetting on the site; this makes questions and answers readable and professional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content licensing and data availability
rubrics_metrics.description: All contributed content is under the same Creative Commons license used by Wikipedia; copies of the database are regularly made available for analysis, reproduction, and future proofing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributors should be aware their posts are CC-licensed and that the database is public for reuse and research. This affects reuse, attribution, and archival considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: You can start posting without registering
rubrics_metrics.description: You can start posting questions and answers without registering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The system is designed to make it easy to jump right in; many mathematicians first visit via search and begin by posting. Registration is optional to start, lowering the barrier to contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use MathOverflow when it fits your research workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: MathOverflow is a natural tool for mathematicians because doing mathematics is driven by asking questions; use it when it complements your research workflow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People formulate problems as small focused questions and may find quick, useful answers that lead to new research directions or collaborations. Consider whether the site will genuinely help your research before posting.
